title: Latent Diffusion Model without Variational Autoencoder
one_liner: Use semantic understanding from self-supervised learning directly in diffusion, skipping the lossy VAE middleman.
lead: Diffusion models generate images one step at a time. Normally they work inside a compressed latent space built by a VAE (a small autoencoder that squeezes images down). But VAEs throw away semantic structure - the model does not know which pixels matter for understanding. SVG throws away the VAE and builds diffusion on top of a frozen self-supervised encoder that already understands images semantically, plus a tiny learnable module for fine details. This keeps semantic clarity intact while speeding training.

paras: Diffusion models generate images by starting with pure noise and adding structure step by step. To train fast, most models work inside a compressed 'latent space' - a squished version of the image made by a VAE (a tiny neural network that learns to compress and decompress). The problem: when you compress an image into a much smaller space to save compute, you lose information. A VAE optimizes to reconstruct pixel colors accurately, but it does not care about semantic structure - whether the pixels encode a cat or a dog, which parts matter for understanding.

This creates a mismatch. Diffusion models need to learn which pixels influence which others so they can add structure in a smart order. But the VAE latent space is entangled - the directions in that space do not align with semantic concepts. When the model trains inside this muddled space, it needs many more steps to figure out what goes where. Inference (generating a new image) also gets slow: you need 25 to 256 denoising steps to get good results.

callout.html: VAE compression throws away semantic structure, forcing diffusion to learn in a muddled latent space that needs many steps to produce good images.

panels.title: 1. Semantic structure exists
panels.caption: An image encoder understands cats, dogs, edges, texture. Semantic means concepts are separable.

panels.title: 2. VAE discards it
panels.caption: VAE compresses to small latent space. Semantic axes get scrambled. Directions are tangled.

panels.title: 3. Diffusion gets lost
panels.caption: Tangled space: model does not know which direction changes which concept.

panels.title: 4. SVG preserves semantic axis
panels.caption: Frozen self-supervised encoder keeps semantic structure. Residual branch adds missing details.

panels.title: 5. Diffusion learns fast
panels.caption: Clear semantic space means training converges fast. Inference needs fewer steps.

steps.text: Take a pretrained self-supervised encoder (DINO) that has learned to recognize image concepts without labels. Lock its weights so it cannot change.
Attach a small learnable residual encoder that captures fine-grained texture and details the frozen encoder missed.
Combine frozen semantic features and learned detail features into one latent space, normalized to prevent numerical mismatch.
Train a diffusion model (using flow matching) on this unified latent space. Semantic clarity makes the learning task simpler.
The latent space now supports generation, recognition, and understanding. One space works for many vision tasks.

paras: Instead of working inside a VAE latent space, SVG trains diffusion inside a hybrid latent space built from a frozen semantic encoder plus learned details. The one key change: swap the lossy VAE for a semantically structured self-supervised foundation.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: semantic clarity in latent space
hidden.name: Semantic entanglement
paras: Semantic entanglement measures whether the directions in a latent space align with concepts (a cat, fur, eyes) or are scrambled. In a VAE latent space built only for pixel reconstruction, different semantic directions overlap - moving along one axis slightly changes many concepts at once, confusing the diffusion model. In SVG, the frozen DINO encoder has already learned to separate concepts cleanly during self-supervised pretraining on millions of images without labels.

The paper estimates this by checking whether diffusion training converges fast and whether few-step sampling (5 to 25 steps instead of 256) produces high-quality images. Fast convergence and good few-step results prove the space is semantically clear. They also measure preservation: applying the SVG encoder to recognition tasks (object classification) shows it kept DINO's discriminative power.

heat.caption: Darker means more semantic discriminability. DINO and SVG latents are clear; VAE is entangled.

reads.html: A space is semantically clear when different concepts sit in different directions, so moving along one axis changes only one concept. A space is entangled when the axes are scrambled.
The paper measures semantic discriminability by convergence speed, few-step generation FID scores, and downstream task accuracy (classification, segmentation, detection).

mechanism.h2: Why semantic structure makes diffusion faster
paras: Diffusion works by learning to gradually add structure to noise. At each step, the model learns to recognize 'what is currently noise' and 'what is stable structure' and nudge noise toward structure. When the latent space is semantically organized, this task is easy: stable structure corresponds to real concepts (a cat's head, a wheel). When the space is entangled, the model has to learn which scrambled direction corresponds to which concept - a harder puzzle that takes many more training steps.

SVG's move is to start with semantic structure that already exists (from self-supervised pretraining), not to learn it from scratch inside a VAE. The frozen DINO encoder brings in millions of images' worth of semantic knowledge. The small residual encoder adds missing details (edges, textures) that semantic understanding alone does not capture. Combining them creates a space where the diffusion model can immediately recognize semantic concepts, so it focuses on learning how to remove noise cleanly, not on figuring out which directions correspond to which concepts.

stages.s: Frozen DINO encoder extracts semantic concepts
Diffusion model denoises in this unified space

math.words: The model learns to predict the velocity (rate of change) of a noisy sample as it moves toward clean. Starting from clean image x0 and noise epsilon, the model observes xt = (1-t)x0 + t*epsilon at step t, where t ranges from 0 (clean) to 1 (pure noise). The velocity vt is the direction from x0 toward pure noise. The model theta is trained to predict this velocity given xt and t.
symbols: the model's predicted velocity direction at step t
the noisy sample at step t (mix of clean image and noise)
the true velocity direction (from clean toward noise)
a weighting that emphasizes certain steps (e.g., penalizing mistakes in the middle more)
average loss over all images and all time steps

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine at step t=0.5, the model sees x_t = 0.5 * clean_image + 0.5 * noise_tensor.
True velocity v_t is the direction from clean toward pure noise (they differ by moving halfway).
Model predicts v_theta = a guess at that direction, magnitude 0.48 (close but not exact).
Averaged over thousands of images and steps, the model learns to predict v_t accurately, so diffusion can reverse noise into images.

math.note: The model learns which way points toward structure (the true velocity). In a semantic latent space, moving in one direction changes one concept clearly; the model does not have to guess, so it learns faster because each weight update points in the right direction.

charts.title: Standard diffusion in VAE space
charts.note: VAE space is entangled: moving one direction scrambles many concepts at once, so training is slow and requires many sampling steps. Recognition tasks suffer because the VAE threw away semantic structure.

charts.title: SVG (this paper)
rows: Sampling steps for good quality (25 steps)
charts.note: Semantic structure accelerates training: each adjustment to the weights moves the model closer to the solution because concepts are clear. Few-step sampling works because the model already knows which direction is which, so it does not waste steps guessing. Recognition tasks work because DINO features are preserved.

items.b: Mismatch between DINO features and residual details.
items.html: DINO and the residual encoder produce numbers on different scales. If not normalized, the decoder over-relies on one and ignores the other. The fix: normalize per-channel during training and jointly train both components.

A semantic encoder trained on classification does not learn to encode every texture or edge. Hallucinations can occur if the residual encoder is too small or if training does not allocate enough capacity to detail capture.
DINO features are high-dimensional. Diffusion training in high dimensions is generally noisy. The fix: use QK-Norm (a normalization technique) and stable diffusion optimizers (e.g., SiT).

items.b: Done right, SVG is stable and fast.
items.html: When all components are normalized and jointly trained with a stable optimizer, diffusion trains reliably in semantic latent space because the space does not have to be learned from scratch - it already encodes concepts. The model converges in fewer epochs because each weight adjustment pushes in the right direction (the concepts are already clear), and produces images as good as VAE baselines while training 10x faster.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal example: use a frozen pretrained DINO encoder from a public checkpoint and a small residual encoder (a single neural network layer that processes image information). Train diffusion on ImageNet 32x32 for a few epochs. Track convergence speed (loss per epoch) and few-step generation quality (FID-50K, a number measuring image realism, at 5, 10, and 25 denoising steps). Compare to a standard VAE-based diffusion baseline on the same hardware and epoch count.
demo.metric_eq: few_step_FID = FID_50K measured after 25 denoising steps
demo.closing: The demo proves that semantic structure from DINO allows diffusion to learn which direction removes which kind of noise more reliably, because the space already tells the model which concepts go where: each weight adjustment moves toward the right solution. Convergence is visibly faster per epoch because the model does not waste time guessing, and few-step sampling works when it fails for VAE baselines because the model already knows which direction is which.
